note: Finds only 13 percent of 77 frameworks include all four components and only 19.5 percent name an oversight mechanism, a strong figure for an audit finding.
title: Governance for safe and responsible AI in healthcare organisations: a scoping review of frameworks

reading.body:
Most published frameworks for governing AI in hospitals are incomplete: only 13 percent of 77 cover principles, assessment, lifecycle, and oversight together, and only 19.5 percent name an oversight mechanism.

The pattern is a gap between stated principles and operational machinery. Frameworks that describe values are common. Frameworks that say who watches the system, at what stage, and against what test are rare. Oversight is the least frequent of the four components, which means the part most tied to accountability is the part most often missing.

This matters for AI specifically because a deployed clinical model changes after deployment. Its inputs drift, its site changes, and its failure modes are not visible from a principles document. A framework without lifecycle stages and oversight cannot catch that. The review's own conclusion points the same way: implementation and evaluation in real settings, not principles alone.

The data covers 77 frameworks for acute care, drawn from three databases in April 2024 and March 2025. It does not say whether any framework was adopted, funded, or enforced, and it does not measure outcomes in patients. It also does not connect governance quality to compute, buildings, or power, and nothing here supports that link. The finding is about documents, not about what hospitals actually run.

explain_beginner: A 2026 review in NPJ Digital Medicine examined 77 existing plans for governing artificial intelligence in hospitals and acute care. The researchers checked whether each plan covered four things: ethical or governance rules, ways to assess AI, stages in an AI system's life, and oversight. Only 10 plans, about 13 percent, covered all four. Oversight was rarest, found in 15 plans, about 19.5 percent. Many plans did not fit real healthcare settings. This matters because hospitals need practical rules and clear oversight, not just broad principles, before these tools are used in care.
explain_business: For healthcare leaders, this review suggests that most published frameworks for AI governance are not ready for operational use. Among 77 frameworks for acute care, only 10, about 13 percent, covered all four needed areas: principles, assessment, lifecycle stages, and oversight. Just 15, about 19.5 percent, named an oversight mechanism. That gap means an organisation cannot assume a framework on paper will provide oversight or fit its real setting. Executives should ask whether any adopted AI governance plan includes clear oversight, practical assessment, and lifecycle controls, and should fund implementation and measurement of impact in real settings rather than relying on principles alone.
explain_practitioner: Wang and colleagues performed a review of existing literature using PRISMA-ScR. They looked in MEDLINE, Embase, and Scopus in April 2024, then again in March 2025, for frameworks that govern AI in acute care. They found 77 frameworks and checked four areas: ethical or governance principles, assessment approaches, stages in an AI system's lifecycle, and oversight. Most did not suit real healthcare settings and missed important parts. Ten frameworks, 13.0 percent, had all four areas. Oversight was least common, appearing in 15 frameworks, 19.5 percent. The authors urge implementation and evaluation in real settings, not just principles.
